summary: At Jericho, Zacchaeus — wealthy chief tax collector and a man the crowd calls a sinner — climbs to see Jesus. Jesus says he ‘must’ stay at his house today; Zacchaeus responds with large-scale giving and restitution, and Jesus announces present salvation to this son of Abraham. Because people expect God's kingdom immediately near Jerusalem, Jesus tells of a nobleman who receives kingship despite citizen hatred, returns, rewards productive servants, rebukes fearful storage, and orders opponents killed — a politically charged story that warns about accountability without making every royal act a portrait of Jesus. Jesus then goes up, enters Jerusalem as a praised king, weeps over the city's missed peace and coming siege, drives commerce from the temple, and teaches daily while leaders seek a way to destroy him.
whyItMatters: Luke's journey reaches its city through a transformed household and a weeping king. Salvation changes money and belonging ‘today’; kingdom expectation must survive delay and accountability; royal arrival brings peace rather than denial of judgment, and temple confrontation begins under the shadow of the siege Jesus foretells (19:43-44).

context.author: The Gospel's anonymous author, traditionally Luke, closing the travel narrative and opening Jerusalem conflict with distinctive Zacchaeus and mina material
context.audience: Theophilus and a wider Greek-reading audience; the chapter connects repentance, wealth, delayed kingdom, kingship, judgment, and temple
context.date: Commonly dated after Jerusalem's destruction in AD 70, around AD 80–90; dates in the 60s and into the early second century are also defended
context.setting: Jericho, a wealthy household, the ascent through Bethphage and Bethany, Mount of Olives, Jerusalem's approach, and temple
context.literaryForm: Call and restitution story, throne-claim parable, royal entry, prophetic lament, symbolic temple action, and conflict summary

outline.heading: Zacchaeus seen, hosted, and restored as Abraham's son
outline.note: A chief tax collector climbs a sycamore; Jesus says he must stay at his house, and Zacchaeus gives half his goods to the poor

outline.heading: Mina parable: delayed rule, entrusted work, and severe judgment
outline.note: A nobleman returns as king; two servants gained minas and are put over cities; one hid his mina and loses it

outline.heading: Ascent, colt, and royal acclamation
outline.note: Disciples bring a colt, saying 'The Lord needs it'; cloaks line the road; Pharisees object, and he says the stones would cry out

outline.heading: Jesus weeps over missed peace and coming siege
outline.note: Near the city, he weeps, saying the things for its peace are hidden; enemies will build a barricade and leave no stone on another

outline.heading: Temple action, daily teaching, and leaders' plot
outline.note: He drives sellers from the temple, calling it a 'den of robbers'; leaders seek to destroy him, but the people hang on his words

keyVerses.text: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.”
keyVerses.why: On one common reading, Zacchaeus becomes the living conclusion to Luke 15's searching and saving movement.

keyVerses.text: saying, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest!”
keyVerses.why: Luke's entry acclamation explicitly names the king and echoes the infancy song's peace and glory.

keyVerses.text: saying to them, “It is written, ‘My house is a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a ‘den of robbers’!”
keyVerses.why: Isaiah's prayer-house (Isaiah 56:7) and Jeremiah's robber-den indictment (Jeremiah 7:11) interpret the temple action as prophetic judgment.

questions.question: Why was Zacchaeus especially hated?
questions.answer: A chief tax collector was head over other tax collectors in Roman-ruled Judea, a job open to collecting more than was due (3:13). Luke also calls him rich, linking office and wealth. The crowd's grievance has moral context, yet its total label ‘sinner’ cannot see the possibility of restitution and restored kinship.

questions.question: Why does Jesus say he ‘must’ stay at Zacchaeus's house?
questions.answer: Dei marks divine necessity throughout Luke. Jesus's self-invitation is not convenience; seeking the lost belongs to God's purpose, and ‘today’ makes that purpose present at a compromised person's table. Hospitality becomes the site of accountability rather than a reward after public respectability.

questions.question: Is Zacchaeus promising new behavior or defending what he already does?
questions.answer: Both Greek verbs, ‘I give’ and ‘I restore,’ are in the present tense; readers differ on whether they describe present practice or a pledge beginning now. The crowd's accusation and Jesus's ‘Today, salvation has come’ favor a transformative public commitment, though habitual-practice readings exist. Either way, his relation to wealth is offered as evidence, not a purchase price for grace.

questions.question: What does fourfold repayment mean?
questions.answer: Torah required differentiated restitution, reaching four- or fivefold in certain theft cases (Exodus 22:1; compare 22:4 and Leviticus 6:5). Zacchaeus combines half his goods given to the poor with maximum-like repayment for extortion. Repentance names harmed parties and material repair rather than stopping at private regret.

questions.question: Is the violent nobleman simply Jesus in disguise?
questions.answer: The plot resembles Archelaus, Herod's son, in Rome, where a Jewish embassy came to petition Caesar against his rule (Josephus, Antiquities 17.11.1), and the ruler's slaughter is morally disturbing. Some features parallel Jesus's departure, return, and judgment; others expose brutal kingship. Parables can press accountability through an unjust or severe character without making every action divine approval.

questions.question: Why punish the servant who safely stored the mina?
questions.answer: The servant acts from a declared image of the ruler as harsh and returns exactly what was entrusted, refusing productive participation. The ruler judges him by his own words. The story warns against fear disguised as caution during kingdom delay, but it should not be used to sanctify exploitative financial return.

questions.question: Why does Jesus weep if Jerusalem is judged?
questions.answer: He desires the city to recognize ‘the things which belong to your peace,’ then describes a barricade, encirclement, and children dashed to the ground, language many readers connect with Jerusalem's destruction in AD 70. Tears prevent judgment from being read as ethnic hatred or divine gloating. The Jewish Messiah laments his beloved Jewish city from within its prophetic tradition.

questions.question: What is a ‘den of robbers’?
questions.answer: In Jeremiah 7:9-11 the robbers steal and murder, then stand in the temple and say, ‘We are delivered.’ Jesus combines Isaiah's house of prayer with Jeremiah's temple sermon against people using sanctuary as protection while practicing injustice. The action concerns corrupted worship and judgment, more than a complaint that individual prices were slightly high.

glossary.def: Head over other tax collectors (19:2), in a job open to collecting more than was due (3:13).
Unit of money, about one sixtieth of a talent, entrusted to servants in the parable.
Psalm acclamation meaning originally ‘save, please’; Luke's entry wording instead foregrounds king and peace.
Prophetic image of sanctuary used as refuge by people whose injustice continues.
